Conclude with a hands-on challenge to add a jump feature using `Input.GetKeyDown()`.

screens.title: Basic Input and Movement with C#
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how Unity senses player intent and converts it into movement that feels consistent on any machine. We start with Unity's Input class to detect keys and mouse actions, and compare simple key checks with axis-based input that produces smoother values. Then we connect that input to the Transform component so your objects actually move. Crucially, we'll introduce Time. deltaTime so movement becomes units per second rather than units per frame. You'll see a working PlayerMovement script, test it in a small scene with a cube and plane, and run a quick experiment to observe what happens when Time. deltaTime is missing. Finally, we'll highlight common mistakes such as treating input as frames instead of time and choosing position changes that ignore local rotation. By the end you'll be able to write a small script that reads horizontal and vertical input, moves and rotates a GameObject, and behaves the same on slow and fast frame rates. Ready to make your first interactive object?

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Basic Input and Movement with C#

Use Unity's Input class to read keyboard and mouse, translate that into movement via Transform, and guard movement with Time.deltaTime for fair, consistent gameplay.

Concept Map
Input → Translate → Time
Input
GetKey, GetAxis, mouse state
Transform
Translate or Rotate relative to facing
DeltaTime
Convert units per frame → units per second
Result
Smooth, consistent movement
Explore Key Topics
Input Methods

GetKey family for presses and GetAxis for smooth values mapped in the Input Manager.

Movement

Use Transform.Translate or transform.position with rotation-aware moves for directional control.

Frame Independence

Multiply by Time.deltaTime so moveSpeed is understood as units per second.

screens.title: Unity's Input class
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Input class is the centralized A P I for reading player controls: keyboard keys, mouse buttons and position, gamepad sticks, and touch. At its simplest, you read booleans that tell you whether a key is held, was pressed this frame, or was released. Input is authoritative for gameplay: your scripts ask it at each Update to decide actions. A concrete example is checking Input. GetKey(KeyCode. W) to move forward while a key is held. A common misconception is that input is event-driven in Unity like UI frameworks; it is polled each frame from Update, so you must decide whether to handle a one-frame event or continuous hold. When you need a single press, use GetKeyDown so the action happens only on the initial frame. When you need to react to a release, use GetKeyUp. For mouse state, GetMouseButton and its Down/Up variants are similar. Remember also Input. mousePosition returns a screen-space pixel position you can use for aiming or UI interaction. Why this matters: correct input handling prevents actions from firing too often or missing because you chose the wrong polling method. Try this: add a debug log that prints true for the exact frame GetKeyDown returns true and observe how it differs from GetKey while you hold the key. That contrast cements the concept.

keyIdea.title: Input polling

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Input Class
Definition

Input methods you will use

  • Input.GetKey() — true while key is held for continuous actions.
  • Input.GetKeyDown() — true only in the frame the key is first pressed.
  • Input.GetKeyUp() — true only in the frame the key is released.
  • Input.GetMouseButton() — mouse buttons, with Down/Up variants.
Common mistake

Using GetKey for a single-press action causes repeated triggers every frame while held instead of once.

Concrete example
// Example check in Update()
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
{
  // Jump once when pressed
  Debug.Log("Jump pressed this frame");
}

if (Input.GetKey(KeyCode.W))
{
  // Move forward while held
  Debug.Log("Moving forward");
}
Check your understanding

Run the scene and hold Space: observe GetKeyDown logs only once, GetKey logs every frame while held.

screens.title: GetKey vs GetAxis
screens.narratorSegment: GetKey family methods and Input. GetAxis serve different purposes. Use GetKey when you need a boolean that tells you a key is held; it's simple and precise. GetAxis returns a float between -1 and 1 and is ideal when you want smooth, analog-like input even from digital sources. For example, Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") maps A and D or left and right arrows into a single float where pressing A produces approximately -1 and pressing D produces approximately 1. This blending lets you create gradual acceleration or feed values into physics or animation systems that expect floats. A common misunderstanding is thinking GetAxis is only for gamepads; the Input Manager maps keyboard keys into axes so they benefit from smoothing and dead zones. Concrete example: use GetKey(KeyCode. W) for a single-action feature like sprint toggled while held, but use GetAxis("Vertical") to compute a movement vector that feels smooth when keys are pressed or released. To test, print the axis value while you press and release keys and notice the float changing rather than jumping instantly. That behavior enables better character feel without extra interpolation code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › GetKey vs GetAxis
GetKey

Boolean, frame-polled

Great for continuous hold checks or single-frame events when paired with Down/Up variants.

Misuse

Using GetKey for smooth motion requires manual interpolation; prefer GetAxis when smoothing is desired.

GetAxis

Float between -1 and 1

Returns smooth values for Horizontal and Vertical axes, useful for movement vectors and rotation input.

Concrete example
float horizontal = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
float vertical = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");
Vector3 movement = new Vector3(horizontal, 0f, vertical);

Observe the axis values change smoothly as keys are pressed and released.

screens.title: Transform.Translate and movement vectors
screens.narratorSegment: The Transform component stores a GameObject's position, rotation, and scale. To move an object in code, you can adjust transform. position directly or use Transform. Translate to move by a vector. Translate is especially useful when you want movement relative to the object's facing direction because it respects local rotation by default. For example, transform. Translate(Vector3. forward * speed * Time. deltaTime) moves the object forward based on where it's facing. A common misconception is that transform. position += movement and Translate are always equivalent. They can be, but direct position changes are absolute and can ignore the object's local orientation unless you calculate direction using transform. forward. Translate provides a convenience for relative moves and can accept a Space. World or Space. Self parameter to disambiguate coordinate space. In practice, for player movement that follows facing, calculate a direction vector such as transform. forward * verticalInput, then either Translate with Space. World or add to position after transforming the vector. The practical takeaway is: prefer Translate for readable relative moves, and ensure Time. deltaTime multiplies any speed to keep motion consistent across frame rates.

keyIdea.title: Relative movement
keyIdea.text: Use Transform.Translate for movement that should follow a GameObject's facing; prefer explicit Space.World when you need world coordinates.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Transform.Translate
What it is

Move by vector relative to space

Translate moves a GameObject by a vector and respects local rotation unless you specify world space.

// Move forward relative to facing
transform.Translate(Vector3.forward * speed * Time.deltaTime);

// Move in world space
transform.Translate(direction * speed * Time.deltaTime, Space.World);
Example

Create a vector from input and move the object relative to its forward direction so 'forward' always follows facing.

Key takeaway

Translate simplifies relative moves; decide Space.World versus Space.Self based on whether movement should ignore local rotation.

screens.title: Why Time.deltaTime matters
screens.narratorSegment: Update runs once per frame, and frame rates vary across machines. Without compensation, moving an object by a fixed amount inside Update makes that movement dependent on frames per second: higher FPS yields more updates per second and therefore more movement. Time. deltaTime gives the elapsed time since the last frame, letting you scale movement by real time instead of frames. For instance, transform. Translate(direction * speed * Time. deltaTime) makes speed represent units per second. A practical experiment is to remove Time. deltaTime temporarily and observe that a fast machine moves objects much further per second than a slow machine. Another misconception is that Time. deltaTime is only for movement; it's also essential for any time-based effect like interpolation, animation progress, or cooldown timers. When using physics in FixedUpdate, you should use Time. fixedDeltaTime instead. In this chapter's simple movement scripts we use Update and Time. deltaTime together. The core rule to remember is: when Update controls a change over time, multiply by Time. deltaTime to ensure consistency and fairness across hardware. Why Time.deltaTime matters means multiply by time.deltatime in update so values become time-based rather than frame-based and movement is consistent.. In practical terms, convert frame updates into units-per-second for fair gameplay. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Multiply by Time.deltaTime in Update so values become time-based rather than frame-based and movement is consistent.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Time.deltaTime
Problem

Frame-dependent movement

If you change position by units per Update, faster machines run Update more often and move farther per second.

// Wrong: frame-dependent
transform.Translate(direction * speed);

// Correct: time-based
transform.Translate(direction * speed * Time.deltaTime);
Experiment

Remove Time.deltaTime and run the scene on different machines or simulate low FPS. Observe the speed difference to internalize why deltaTime is required.

Pro tip

When using physics-based movement, use fixed update timing with fixedDeltaTime instead of Update's deltaTime.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: Read axis values, build a direction vector with transform.forward, apply Translate with Time.deltaTime, and rotate with Rotate using horizontal input.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › PlayerMovement Script
Core script
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f; // Units per second
    public float rotationSpeed = 100f; // Degrees per second

    void Update()
    {
        // Get input for horizontal and vertical movement (WASD or Arrow Keys)
        float horizontalMovement = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); // A/D or Left/Right Arrows
        float verticalMovement = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");   // W/S or Up/Down Arrows

        // Calculate movement direction relative to the player's forward direction
        Vector3 movementDirection = transform.forward * verticalMovement;

        // Apply movement
        transform.Translate(movementDirection * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime, Space.World); // Move in world space

        // Rotate the player based on horizontal input
        transform.Rotate(Vector3.up * horizontalMovement * rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
    }
}
Annotations
  • Public fields let you tune speed values in the Inspector while testing.
  • GetAxis provides smooth input values for building a Vector3 movement vector.
  • transform.forward ensures forward moves relative to facing direction.
  • Time.deltaTime converts moveSpeed into units per second for consistent motion.
  • Rotate updates facing so movementDirection changes naturally next frame.
Check

While playing, change moveSpeed and rotationSpeed in the Inspector to feel how they affect motion immediately.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Hands-on: Cube
Steps
  1. Create a new Basic scene.
  2. Right-click Hierarchy → 3D Object → Cube. Set Position to 0, 0.5, 0.
  3. Right-click Hierarchy → 3D Object → Plane. Set Position 0,0,0 and Scale 5,1,5.
  4. Add Rigidbody to the Cube and uncheck Use Gravity.
Script & Test
  1. Create PlayerMovement.cs, paste the movement code, and attach it to the cube.
  2. Adjust the Main Camera (for example, X:0 Y:10 Z:-10, Rotation X:45) to view the cube.
  3. Run the scene and use WASD or arrow keys. Tune moveSpeed and rotationSpeed in the Inspector while running.
Experiment

Temporarily remove *Time.deltaTime from Translate or Rotate and observe how the cube's speed changes with frame rate. Put Time.deltaTime back when finished to restore fair movement.

screens.title: Alternate: forward movement and world space
screens.narratorSegment: The example code computes movementDirection as transform. forward multiplied by vertical input so forward movement always follows the cube's facing. If you instead used Vector3. forward the cube would move along world Z regardless of its rotation. Using transform. Translate(movementDirection * moveSpeed * Time. deltaTime, Space. World) moves the cube in world space by a world-space vector that was already rotated by transform. forward. The pattern separates concerns: compute direction in local terms, then apply movement in world coordinates to avoid accumulating local-space offsets in unexpected ways. Rotation uses transform. Rotate(Vector3. up * horizontalMovement * rotationSpeed * Time. deltaTime) which rotates the object about its local Y axis by degrees scaled per second. Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Forward & Space
Compute direction

transform.forward is the object's forward in world space after rotation. Multiply it by vertical input to move forward relative to facing.

Vector3 movementDirection = transform.forward * verticalMovement;
transform.Translate(movementDirection * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime, Space.World);
Why Space.World?

We pass a world-space vector and ask Translate to move in world space to avoid unexpected local stacking. Use Space.Self when you want Translate to interpret the input vector in the object's local coordinates directly.

screens.title: Mouse input and mousePosition

GetMouseButton, GetMouseButtonDown, and GetMouseButtonUp, mirroring keyboard methods: GetMouseButton(0) checks the left button while the Down and Up variants detect single-frame press or release. screens.title: Debugging movement issues
screens.narratorSegment: When movement behaves oddly, a few systematic checks usually reveal the cause. First, verify Time. deltaTime is present in Translate or Rotate calls; missing it produces frame-rate dependent speeds. Second, confirm you are using the intended coordinate space: Vector3. forward moves in world space, transform. forward moves relative to the object's rotation. Third, check whether physics or gravity is interfering: a Rigidbody with Use Gravity enabled will move under physics unless you intentionally control it. Fourth, ensure input method choice matches the action: use GetKeyDown for single events like jumping and GetAxis for continuous smooth motion. A typical debugging workflow is to add Debug. Log lines to print input values such as axis floats and booleans to confirm the values you expect at runtime. For rotation issues, print transform. eulerAngles after rotating to confirm sign and axis. These checks are lightweight and often point directly to the error so you can fix code quickly and re-run the scene to validate the outcome. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how Unity senses player intent and converts it into movement that feels consistent on any machine. We start with Unity's Input class to detect keys and mouse actions, and compare simple key checks with axis-based input that produces smoother values. Then we connect that input to the Transform component so your objects actually move. Crucially, we'll introduce Time. deltaTime so movement becomes units per second rather than units per frame. You'll see a working PlayerMovement script, test it in a small scene with a cube and plane, and run a quick experiment to observe what happens when Time. deltaTime is missing. Finally, we'll highlight common mistakes such as treating input as frames instead of time and choosing position changes that ignore local rotation. By the end you'll be able to write a small script that reads horizontal and vertical input, moves and rotates a GameObject, and behaves the same on slow and fast frame rates. Ready to make your first interactive object?

By the end of these exercises you will implement basic keyboard and mouse input detection using Unity's Input class. You'll distinguish when to use direct key checks such as GetKey and when to prefer axes via GetAxis. You will translate GameObjects by manipulating their Transform component and understand why Translate is useful when moving relative to an object's rotation. Most importantly, you will apply Time. deltaTime to ensure your movement calculations are frame-rate independent so gameplay feels consistent on different machines. Each objective maps to a small skill: detecting a single press, creating smooth continuous motion, moving relative to facing, and turning frame-dependent motion into units-per-second. These are foundational skills that let you make a player-controlled cube, tune its speed in the Inspector, and test movement behavior. We'll also include micro-mnemonics to help you remember which method to use, and a verified competency milestone for practice. Work through the hands-on activity to connect code and scene results; that will confirm you can both write and test a movement script.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical memory aids and small tests you can run while coding. For input detection, remember the mnemonic: 'Down for single events, Held for continuous' to distinguish GetKeyDown from GetKey. For axis input, recall 'Axis blends keys into smooth values' so you prefer Input. GetAxis when you want analog-like behavior. For Transform movement, think 'Translate follows facing' to remember Translate respects local rotation. For timing, keep the rule 'Always multiply by Time. deltaTime unless movement should be frame-based'. Each mnemonic ties to a quick verification: press the key and watch a console boolean, run the scene and slowly hold keys to confirm GetAxis returns a smooth float, tweak moveSpeed in the Inspector while playing, and deliberately remove Time. deltaTime to see speed change with FPS. These small checks are the verified competency milestones that confirm you can both reason about and test each objective in your Unity scene.

Unity's Input class is the centralized A P I for reading player controls: keyboard keys, mouse buttons and position, gamepad sticks, and touch. At its simplest, you read booleans that tell you whether a key is held, was pressed this frame, or was released. Input is authoritative for gameplay: your scripts ask it at each Update to decide actions. A concrete example is checking Input. GetKey(KeyCode. W) to move forward while a key is held. A common misconception is that input is event-driven in Unity like UI frameworks; it is polled each frame from Update, so you must decide whether to handle a one-frame event or continuous hold. When you need a single press, use GetKeyDown so the action happens only on the initial frame. When you need to react to a release, use GetKeyUp. For mouse state, GetMouseButton and its Down/Up variants are similar. Remember also Input. mousePosition returns a screen-space pixel position you can use for aiming or UI interaction. Why this matters: correct input handling prevents actions from firing too often or missing because you chose the wrong polling method. Try this: add a debug log that prints true for the exact frame GetKeyDown returns true and observe how it differs from GetKey while you hold the key. That contrast cements the concept.

GetKey family methods and Input. GetAxis serve different purposes. Use GetKey when you need a boolean that tells you a key is held; it's simple and precise. GetAxis returns a float between -1 and 1 and is ideal when you want smooth, analog-like input even from digital sources. For example, Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") maps A and D or left and right arrows into a single float where pressing A produces approximately -1 and pressing D produces approximately 1. This blending lets you create gradual acceleration or feed values into physics or animation systems that expect floats. A common misunderstanding is thinking GetAxis is only for gamepads; the Input Manager maps keyboard keys into axes so they benefit from smoothing and dead zones. Concrete example: use GetKey(KeyCode. W) for a single-action feature like sprint toggled while held, but use GetAxis("Vertical") to compute a movement vector that feels smooth when keys are pressed or released. To test, print the axis value while you press and release keys and notice the float changing rather than jumping instantly. That behavior enables better character feel without extra interpolation code.

The Transform component stores a GameObject's position, rotation, and scale. To move an object in code, you can adjust transform. position directly or use Transform. Translate to move by a vector. Translate is especially useful when you want movement relative to the object's facing direction because it respects local rotation by default. For example, transform. Translate(Vector3. forward * speed * Time. deltaTime) moves the object forward based on where it's facing. A common misconception is that transform. position += movement and Translate are always equivalent. They can be, but direct position changes are absolute and can ignore the object's local orientation unless you calculate direction using transform. forward. Translate provides a convenience for relative moves and can accept a Space. World or Space. Self parameter to disambiguate coordinate space. In practice, for player movement that follows facing, calculate a direction vector such as transform. forward * verticalInput, then either Translate with Space. World or add to position after transforming the vector. The practical takeaway is: prefer Translate for readable relative moves, and ensure Time. deltaTime multiplies any speed to keep motion consistent across frame rates.

Update runs once per frame, and frame rates vary across machines. Without compensation, moving an object by a fixed amount inside Update makes that movement dependent on frames per second: higher FPS yields more updates per second and therefore more movement. Time. deltaTime gives the elapsed time since the last frame, letting you scale movement by real time instead of frames. For instance, transform. Translate(direction * speed * Time. deltaTime) makes speed represent units per second. A practical experiment is to remove Time. deltaTime temporarily and observe that a fast machine moves objects much further per second than a slow machine. Another misconception is that Time. deltaTime is only for movement; it's also essential for any time-based effect like interpolation, animation progress, or cooldown timers. When using physics in FixedUpdate, you should use Time. fixedDeltaTime instead. In this chapter's simple movement scripts we use Update and Time. deltaTime together. The core rule to remember is: when Update controls a change over time, multiply by Time. deltaTime to ensure consistency and fairness across hardware. Why Time.deltaTime matters means multiply by time.deltatime in update so values become time-based rather than frame-based and movement is consistent.. In practical terms, convert frame updates into units-per-second for fair gameplay. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
